column2: Reuben and Gad have a very great multitude of livestock; the repeated abundance motivates their assessment of Jazer and Gilead.
Both tribes approach Moses, Eleazar and the congregation's rulers; all recipients remain.
The nine requested places remain Ataroth, Dibon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, Elealeh, Sibmah, Nebo and Beon in source order.
The land's suitability for livestock and the servants' ownership of livestock complete the petition's rationale.
The request combines an eastern possession with not being made to cross Jordan; both clauses remain petitions to Moses.
Moses contrasts their brothers going to war with their sitting here, preserving the rebuking question.
Turning Israel's minds away from crossing into the Lord's gift is explicitly challenged.
The fathers' mission from Kadesh-barnea is recalled as a question, not inserted as an independent narrative.
The Ravine of the Cluster, examination of the land and discouragement of entry remain causally connected.
The Lord's fierce anger and oath introduce the quoted exclusion.
The oath excludes those twenty and older who know evil and good; Abraham, Isaac and Jacob remain all three named recipients of the promise.
Caleb is the one set apart, not a substituted ethnic epithet; Joshua is also excepted, and the selected singular followed remains he.
Whirled them about preserves the forceful selected verb, with forty years and consumption of the wrongdoing generation both retained.
The new generation is a band of sinful men adding to the Lord's anger against Israel, without a softened label.
Turning away brings renewed abandonment in the wilderness and wrongdoing against the entire congregation.
column3: The pronoun chain involves collective Israel; the inherited plural them is intelligible, but precise agency through the infinitival construction merits grammatical review.

column2: The tribes propose sheepfolds for livestock and towns for dependents, preserving the two distinct provisions.
They offer themselves as an armed advance guard until Israel reaches its place; the dependents remain in walled towns because of local inhabitants.
The emphatic refusal to return home lasts until every Israelite receives an inheritance.
They disclaim a further western inheritance because their eastern allotments have been received; the directional distinction remains explicit.
Moses' response begins conditional assent and requires equipping themselves before the Lord for war.
Every armed man must cross until the Lord's enemy is removed from before Him; the divine pronouns remain connected.
Subjection of the land precedes return and guiltlessness toward the Lord and Israel; before the Lord is deliberately repeated.
They will recognize their sin when evils overtake them, preserving the selected construction rather than substituting the familiar sin-will-find-you formula.
Towns and folds may be built, but their spoken promise must be performed.
The tribes call Moses our lord while describing themselves as servants; human address remains ordinary you rather than Thou.
Dependents, wives and all livestock remain in Gilead's towns; the three groups are not collapsed.
All servants will cross armed and in formation before the Lord, in accordance with Moses' words.
Eleazar, Joshua and the tribal ancestral-house rulers are named for carrying out the arrangement.
column3: The selected verb can concern commissioning or commending; the inherited appointed over them should receive further syntactic review before its administrative nuance is treated as settled.

column2: Crossing armed and gaining dominion are conditions for granting the tribes Gilead; all conditions remain.
Failure to cross entails bringing dependents, wives and livestock ahead into Canaan, where the tribes share an inheritance. This longer selected instruction is preserved.
Reuben and Gad answer that they will perform everything their lord says to his servants, retaining Moses as the contextual addressee.
The armed crossing into Canaan is reaffirmed together with the request for the possession across Jordan on the east.
Gad, Reuben and half Manasseh receive the kingdoms of Sihon and Og, with land, towns and boundaries; half Manasseh is not omitted.
Gad's building list opens with Dibon, Ataroth and Aroer in selected order.
Shophar and Jazer remain, with raised them up retained as a separate action rather than replaced by an extra place name.
Nimrah and Beth-haran complete the fortified-town and sheepfold list.
Reuben's building list begins Heshbon, Elealeh and Kiriathaim.
Baal-meon and Sibmah remain with the surrounding and naming clauses; the selected text is not replaced by a renaming prohibition.
column3: With defenses makes the surrounding participle explicit from the fortified-town context; further lexical review should decide whether the noun addition is warranted.

column2: The selected singular a son of Machir is preserved, along with taking Gilead and destroying its Amorite inhabitant.
Moses gives Gilead to Machir son of Manasseh, who settles there; the narrated singular remains.
Jair's capture and naming of the settlements remain, with the descriptive Settlements of Jair rather than a foreign compound.
Nabau captures Kenath and its villages and names them Naboth; the selected difference between the personal and resulting place forms is preserved.
The stations concern Israel's departure with its force under Moses and Aaron, preserving the heading's participants.
Moses records departures and stations through the Lord's word; both travel terms remain in the record's introduction.
The fifteenth of the first month is the day after Passover, and the departure with a high hand occurs before all Egyptians.
Egypt buries all the dead firstborn struck by the Lord, while the Lord also exacts vengeance on their gods.
The first itinerary leg runs Rameses to Succoth; the departure-and-camp formula remains.
Succoth leads to Bouthan, described as part of the wilderness; the selected name is not changed to Etham.
Bouthan leads to the mouth of Eiroth opposite Baal-zephon, with the camp also opposite Migdol; both orientations remain.
The route from Eiroth crosses the sea and traverses wilderness for three days to Bitternesses; the emphatic they themselves remains.
Bitternesses leads to Elim, where twelve springs and seventy palms accompany the waterside camp.
Elim leads to the Red Sea; the intervening coastal station is retained.
The Red Sea leads to the wilderness of Sin, keeping the selected designation.
Sin leads to Raphaka, preserving this selected place form rather than substituting Dophkah.
Raphaka leads to Alush, retaining both endpoints and the repeated camping formula.
Alush leads to Rephidim, with the additional lack of drinking water explicitly retained.
Rephidim leads to the wilderness of Sinai; the mountain-region designation is distinguished from Sin.
Sinai leads to Graves of Craving, translating the selected descriptive place name.
Graves of Craving leads to Hazeroth, retaining the repeated departure point.
Hazeroth leads to Rithmah, preserving the next itinerary leg.
Rithmah leads to Rimmon-perez, retaining the compound place as one station.
Rimmon-perez leads to Lemonah; the selected form is not silently normalized to Libnah.
Lemonah leads to Dessah, preserving the selected place form.
Dessah leads to Makellath; this spelling remains distinct from the later Makheloth station.
Makellath leads to Shaphar, keeping the stated sequence.
Shaphar leads to Haradah, preserving both endpoints.
Haradah leads to Makheloth, distinct in the selected text from Makellath at 33:22–23.
Makheloth leads to Kataath; the inherited selected place form remains.
Kataath leads to Tarath, with no normalization to a different familiar itinerary name.
Tarath leads to Mithkah, the inherited conventional spelling corresponding to the selected Matekka form.
Mithkah leads to Zalmonah; this selected station is preserved even though the same name recurs later.
Zalmonah leads to Moseroth, retaining the selected route rather than changing its preceding station.
Moseroth leads to Banaia, preserving the selected form without expanding it to a familiar Hebrew compound.
Banaia leads to Mount Gadgad, retaining Mount as part of the selected description.
Mount Gadgad leads to Jotbathah, the inherited conventional rendering of the selected Etebatha form.
Jotbathah leads to Abronah, retaining the next station without geographical harmonization.
Abronah leads to Ezion-geber, preserving the complete departure-and-camp formula.
Two legs remain within this single stored unit: Ezion-geber to Sin, then Sin to Paran, identified as Kadesh. Neither leg is omitted.
Kadesh leads to Hor the mountain near Edom, retaining the geographical qualification.
Aaron ascends at the Lord's command and dies in year forty, month five, day one; all date components remain.
Aaron's age is one hundred twenty-three at death on Hor, keeping both age and place.
The Canaanite king of Arad hears during Israel's entry; the inherited finite clause makes the selected participial sentence readable without supplying a new action.
Hor leads to Zalmonah, retaining the second occurrence of this selected name in the itinerary.
Zalmonah leads to Phino, without substituting a familiar alternative place spelling.
Phino leads to Oboth; the recurring itinerary formula remains intact.
Oboth leads to Gai on the other side at Moab's borders, preserving both qualifications.
Gai leads to Dibon-Gad, retaining the compound destination.
Dibon-Gad leads to Gelmon-diblathaim, preserving the selected first component rather than replacing it with Almon.
Gelmon-diblathaim leads to the mountains of Abarim opposite Nebo, retaining the plural mountains and orientation.
Abarim leads to the western side of Moab by the Jordan opposite Jericho; the selected western wording is not normalized to plains.
The camp spans Aisimoth to Belshittim beside Jordan on Moab's western side, preserving the selected endpoints.
The Lord speaks to Moses in the same western-Moab setting by Jordan opposite Jericho.
The message identifies Israel's crossing into Canaan before giving its commands.
Inhabitants, lookout places, cast idols and pillars receive distinct destruction or removal commands; selected lookout places is not silently changed to high places.
Destruction of the inhabitants and settlement in their land are repeated, with the Lord's gift as allotment stated as the reason.
Tribal allotment by lot is scaled to group size, while the place where a name comes out belongs to that recipient; all allocation principles remain.
Survivors become splinters in eyes and missiles in sides and act as enemies, preserving all three selected images or actions.
The Lord threatens to do to Israel what He had determined for the inhabitants, retaining the reversal without expansion.
